newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Council debates tough 1997 budget with parliament.
newsitem.headline: Council debates tough 1997 budget with parliament.

text.p: The Budget Council met members of the European Parliament on Tuesday to negotiate an unprecedented zero growth 1997 budget plan and debate issues pertaining to the legal bases of future expenditure.
Diplomats said the two sides would focus their attention on parliament's proposal for a special reserve of 300 million Ecus to finance TENs and a programme for Northern Ireland.
Several large member states, in particular Germany and Britain, were said to be strongly against such a reserve.
The battle over additional money for TENs has been at the heart of the European Commission's plans to spur greater employment growth.
The Commission has argued that more money is needed to complete the large infrastructure projects, which include an extension of high speed rail links across Europe.
But the Budget Council and the ECOFIN have repeatedly rejected the appeals, arguing that insufficient funds were not responsible for the slow pace of completion.

Overall, the ministers will propose a budget for 1997 worth 88.585 billion Ecus in commitments and 81.790 billion Ecus in payments. This compares with 1996 commitments of 86.580 billion Ecus and payments of 81.943 billion Ecus.

Another issue up for consideration is the legal bases for future expenditure. Both the Council, the parliament and the Commission have agreed there should be legal bases for certain kinds of spending.

Specificially, the text proposed by parliament says, "In accordance with Article 22 of the Financial Regulation, the implementation of budget appropriations for all significant actions requires prior adoption of a legal basis."
This would not apply to spending in the reserve.
The desire to have a legal base for certain types of expenditure stems in part from the proliferation of programmes which have often carried on well beyond their initial time horizon.

Both the Council and the parliament agree that spending programmes which have a limited objective -- a pilot scheme or emergency aid, for example -- but stretch beyond two years would require legal justification.
Without one the spending could be halted.

The ministers will also consider the costs of eradicating mad cow disease. When the parliament last discussed the budget in October, there was no agreement on allocating future funds to help beef farmers through the crisis caused by the disease, properly called bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE).
The parliament will take up the EU's budget plan again in December, at which point it becomes final. Typically, the parliament reinstates the cuts the ministers propose.
